kurz: How financial independence can be calculated as the ratio of investment income to living costs, and why spending has a greater effect than returns.

bloecke.md:
Financial independence can be described as a ratio: investment income divided by living costs. Once this ratio reaches one, paid work is no longer necessary and becomes voluntary. The denominator, that is, living costs, has a greater effect than the numerator.

If annual spending falls permanently by €3,000, the capital required at a withdrawal rate of 3.5% immediately drops by around €86,000. If you instead save an additional €3,000 a year, it takes almost two decades to achieve the same effect. A robust calculation therefore starts with spending, not with the portfolio.

bloecke.formel: Target capital = Annual spending ÷ Withdrawal rate
bloecke.erklaerung: The reciprocal of the withdrawal rate is the multiplier used in the FIRE discussion. A withdrawal rate of 4% gives 25 times annual spending, 3.5% gives 28.6 times and 3.25% around 31 times.
variablen: all spending in a full year, including insurance, taxes and irregular items
share of the starting assets that is withdrawn in the first year and thereafter only adjusted for inflation

bloecke.md:
## Origin of the 4% rule

In 1994, William Bengen used US market data from 1926 to 1992 to examine which inflation-adjusted withdrawal a mixed portfolio would have survived for thirty years. He arrived at 4% in the first year. With that, the money would have lasted at least 33 years in all the periods examined. The Trinity study confirmed this in 1998 with data from 1926 to 1995 for periods of 15 to 30 years. The figure was then used as a rule and eventually as a target, which often leads to misunderstandings.

Two properties of the rule are often overlooked. First, the withdrawal is rigid. It is set at the start and afterwards only adjusted for inflation, regardless of whether the portfolio is currently rising or has lost a third. Second, a scenario already counts as a success if one euro is left on the last day of the period. The capital is therefore expressly allowed to be used up. Investors who want to preserve their wealth or pass it on have to work with a different withdrawal rate.

- The rule applies to a thirty-year period. If you stop working at 45, the planning covers fifty to sixty years. For such periods, more recent analyses (including the withdrawal rate series by Early Retirement Now) tend to arrive at 3.25% to 3.5%, that is, 29 to 31 times instead of 25 times.
- The rule is based on US data. The American market was the most successful of the 20th century, whereas German capital market history includes two practically complete devaluations (1923, 1948). How much this lowers the safe withdrawal rate for Germany is disputed among experts and cannot be pinned down with a figure here. What is undisputed is that it makes the rate lower.
- The rule takes into account neither taxes nor product costs. In Germany, both are a separate item (see below).
- The rule does not take health insurance into account. In the US, it is tied to the employer; in Germany, to insurance status. In German calculations, it therefore causes the largest gap.

## The influence of the savings rate

The time until independence depends almost entirely on the savings rate and hardly on income. This is because every euro saved works twice. It increases wealth and at the same time lowers the target, because the target is a multiple of spending. If you calculate with constant net income, income cancels out of the equation. The duration then depends only on the savings rate and the real return.

bloecke.titel: Years until independence by savings rate
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with starting assets of zero, a 5% real return and a constant savings rate from net income; the level of income plays no role in the duration.

bloecke.titel: The same calculation in euros at €4,000 net a month

bloecke.md: At a savings rate of 30%, a real return of 6% instead of 5% shortens the duration from around 28 to around 26 years. A savings rate of 40% instead of 30% shortens it, with the same return, from 28 to around 22 years. The return therefore has the smaller influence, and it is the only one of the two variables that you cannot control. The long-term results of global equities help to put the model assumption into perspective. From 1900 to 2024 they delivered around 5.2% a year in real terms, but only around 3.5% in the period from 2000 to 2024.

## Additional items in Germany

The first additional item is health insurance. After leaving employment, you usually become a voluntary member of your statutory health insurance fund and pay the full contribution without an employer's share. For assessing contributions there is a lower limit of one third of the reference value (Bezugsgröße), which means around €1,318 a month in 2026. The reduced contribution rate of 14.0% under Section 243 SGB V (Social Code Book V, health insurance) applies without entitlement to sickness benefit. Together with an average additional contribution of around 2.9% and 3.6% for long-term care insurance (with a child), this comes to around €270 a month, or just over €3,200 a year. This amount is the lower limit, not the norm. For voluntary members, contributions are assessed on their entire economic capacity, which also includes capital income and rental income. Where the line lies between income subject to contributions and a mere reallocation of assets has to be clarified with the fund in each individual case. Above the contribution assessment ceiling (Beitragsbemessungsgrenze) of €5,812.50 a month, the figure is around €1,192 a month, or just under €14,300 a year.

The second item is taxes. A withdrawal is not the same as income, because only the gain portion of the units sold is taxable. For an equity fund, 30% of this remains tax-free thanks to the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung). The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 is deducted from the rest. On the remaining amount, 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) is due, plus 5.5% solidarity surcharge on top of that, 26.375% in total. For a withdrawal of €35,000, half of which consists of gains, this results in around €2,970 in tax a year. After many decades of saving, the gain portion is higher, and so is the tax.

bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation for annual spending of €30,000 and stopping work at 45; all items are derived in the text, and the pension is discounted at 3% real over 22 years.

bloecke.md:
## The statutory pension as an offsetting item

The American calculation assumes a single, continuous withdrawal phase. In Germany, if you stop working early, the portfolio first finances the period until the pension starts, after which the statutory pension is added. Twenty years of employment subject to social security contributions at average earnings result in about twenty earnings points (Entgeltpunkte). At the current pension value (aktueller Rentenwert) of €42.52 per earnings point (from 1 July 2026), that is around €850 gross a month from the standard retirement age of 67. After deducting pensioners' share of health and long-term care insurance, 12.35% in total, around €745 remains. If you stop working at 45 in 2026, the pension begins 22 years later, in 2048. It is then 95% subject to income tax; for pensions starting from 2058, 100%.

The portfolio therefore only has to cover this part of spending until 67. Mathematically, at a 3.5% withdrawal rate the pension corresponds to around €256,000 of capital. If you stop working at 45, that is still just over €133,000 when discounted in real terms. This requires the five-year qualifying period (Wartezeit), without which no pension entitlement arises. Voluntary contributions of between €112.16 and €1,571.70 a month can increase this entitlement later on. Contributions for the previous year can be paid until 31 March.

The annual pension statement (Renteninformation) only gives a projection based on extrapolation assumptions. What is meaningful is the **insurance record** (Versicherungsverlauf), which you can request from Deutsche Rentenversicherung (German statutory pension insurance, DRV). It lists the earnings points credited so far. This number times the current pension value gives your current entitlement in euros per month. Only this figure should go into your own calculation.

## Partial independence

Complete independence without any earned income is the most expensive form, because the capital then has to replace every future source of income. Mathematically, part-time work is the most efficient option, because any remaining income reduces the capital required. A net income of €1,000 a month covers €12,000 of annual spending and, at 3.5%, replaces around €343,000 of wealth. A part-time job subject to social security contributions also keeps health insurance in the affordable range, and earnings points continue to be credited.

The second variant concerns timing. If a portfolio is built up early enough, you can stop saving and let the portfolio grow until the standard retirement age through compound interest alone. The target is then the amount that grows to 28 times spending by 67.

bloecke.unter: Only the upper half requires the full target capital; in the two lower fields, remaining paid work replaces part of it.

felder.text: Full coverage on a tight budget. Smallest target capital, but also the smallest buffer. €300 more in fixed costs a month requires around €103,000 more capital.
Full coverage on a comfortable budget. Annual spending of €60,000 requires around €1.7 million at 3.5%. Income usually matters more than discipline here.
Part-time income covers the gap. €1,000 net a month replaces around €343,000 of capital. Health insurance and the pension account continue.
The portfolio is enough for later and grows without further contributions. Work still covers current costs, but without the pressure to save and usually with fewer hours.

bloecke.md:
Two model portfolios start with €500,000, withdraw €20,000 a year and achieve exactly the same thirty annual returns: five times minus 10% and 25 times plus 8%. As a geometric mean, that is 4.77% a year. The portfolios differ only in the order of the returns.

If the bad years come first, the portfolio is empty in year 28. If they come last, there is around €1.02 million after thirty years. The average return is therefore not a useful planning figure in the withdrawal phase. For this reason, the safe withdrawal rate is well below the expected return. This **sequence-of-returns risk** and the measures against it (a buffer in an instant-access savings account, dynamic withdrawal rules with guardrails, valuation-dependent withdrawal rates) are covered and worked through in the retirement provision module. For the target figure, it is enough to conclude that you should calculate with a safety margin rather than with the average.

## Typical patterns when stopping work

Three patterns appear so regularly in personal accounts that they belong in the planning. The first is postponement out of a need for security. Once the target figure has been reached, another year is added and then another, because the portfolio grows every year and stopping seems safer every year. The second is the loss of daily structure. Besides income, work also provides a fixed rhythm, tasks and most of an adult's social contacts. Planning that considers only the financial side therefore covers only a third of what needs to be planned.

The third pattern is systematically underestimating your own spending. The target figure is based on a budget drawn up during a phase of great discipline, but it has to finance forty years of life. That includes family members needing care, dental treatment, moves and replacing the car, which does not appear in any monthly budget. A target figure derived from twelve months of household accounts instead of three years therefore turns out too low.

The practical value of the calculation rarely lies in stopping work completely. Even wealth of 10 times annual spending strengthens your negotiating position with an employer, allows you to resign without a new contract lined up and makes a change of industry with a pay cut affordable. Part of the benefit therefore arises long before the target figure is reached.

mitnehmen: Every euro of annual spending saved permanently immediately reduces the capital required by 25 to 31 times that amount.
The savings rate determines the time until independence more strongly than the return, and it is the only one of the two variables that you decide yourself.
The 4% rule is a historical US finding for thirty years without taxes and health insurance, not a constant; for fifty years, 29 to 31 times is the more realistic guideline.
In a German calculation, voluntary health insurance and flat-rate withholding tax together form a six-figure capital item, and the statutory pension from 67 partly offsets it.
Mathematically, part-time work is the most efficient option, because €1,000 of remaining monthly income replaces around €343,000 of capital.

begriffe.text: Share of starting assets that is withdrawn in the first year of retirement and thereafter only adjusted for inflation, without the portfolio running out before the end of the planned period. It is based on historical data, is not a guarantee and depends on the period, market, taxes and costs.

The risk that bad market years fall directly after withdrawals begin. Because units then have to be sold at low prices, a portfolio can run out early despite a good average return. For a lump-sum investment without deposits or withdrawals, by contrast, the order of returns makes no difference; with a savings plan, bad years do the most damage towards the end of the accumulation phase, because that is when the most money is invested.

State in which the existing portfolio grows to the target sum by retirement age through capital growth alone. Further contributions are no longer needed; current spending continues to be covered by earned income.

Lower limit from which contributions to voluntary statutory health insurance are calculated. It is one third of the monthly reference value, around €1,318 in 2026. Even insured persons without current income pay contributions on this notional amount.
